text: The president of Tunisia, officially known as the president of the Republic of Tunisia (Arabic: رئيس الجمهورية التونسية, romanized: Ra'īs al-Jumhūriyyah at-Tūnisiyyah), serves as the executive head of state and is the commander-in-chief of the Tunisian Armed Forces. The president exercises executive power in collaboration with a government led by the prime minister under a presidential system. According to the Constitution, the president is elected by direct universal suffrage for a five-year term, renewable once. The first president, Habib Bourguiba, was appointed when the position was created on 25 July 1957 and remained in power for 30 years until he was removed in a coup on 7 November 1987 by his prime minister, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, who then assumed the presidency and ruled for 23 years until his removal during the Tunisian revolution on 14 January 2011. Following Ben Ali’s ousting, Fouad Mebazaa was appointed as interim president until 13 December 2011, when Moncef Marzouki was elected by the Constituent Assembly as the first democratic president in Tunisia’s history. Marzouki handed over power on 31 December 2014 to Beji Caid Essebsi, who won the 2014 presidential election and became the second directly democratically elected president, serving until his death on 25 July 2019. During this period, Parliament Speaker Mohamed Ennaceur temporarily assumed the presidency until new elections were held. Bourguiba and Ben Ali both led the ruling party, initially the Neo Destour, then the Socialist Destourian Party, and later the Democratic Constitutional Rally, from independence in 1956 until the 2011 revolution, when the president must renounce party affiliation upon winning the presidency. The 2022 Tunisian constitutional referendum transformed Tunisia into a presidential republic, granting the president sweeping powers while significantly limiting parliament’s role. The current president, Kais Saied, has held office since 23 October 2019. Since the adoption of a republican constitution in June 1959, Tunisia has had exactly four directly elected presidents. Bourguiba became the first president after the 1957 proclamation of a republic and was formally elected in 1959; he was declared president for life in 1975 and removed in 1987 by Ben Ali, who claimed Bourguiba was medically unfit. Ben Ali served as acting president, was elected in 1989, and remained in power until 2011, when he was ousted during a popular uprising. In the country’s first free presidential election in December 2014, Beji Caid Essebsi was elected in the second round. For much of its history, Tunisia lacked Western-style political democracy and experienced widespread human rights violations, leading to a lack of international credibility in elections such as that of 2009, which saw implausibly high margins for the ruling party, the Constitutional Democratic Rally and its predecessors. Prior to 1999, presidential candidates had to secure endorsements from at least 30 political figures—a barrier only feasible for candidates from the dominant RCD party—making it nearly impossible for opposition figures to gain nominations. Even after the requirement was lifted, Ben Ali was reelected three times with extremely high margins, including a low of 89 percent in 2009. The original constitution granted the president extensive executive and legislative powers, effectively making him a virtual dictator, with no term limits until 1975 when Bourguiba was named president for life. From 1987 to 2002, a president was limited to three five-year terms, with no more than two in a row, but this restriction was abolished in June 2002. The 2014 Constitution preserved the presidency as the central institution but introduced checks and balances to prevent authoritarianism, including a two-term limit—whether consecutive or non-consecutive—explicitly prohibited by the Constitution from being amended. Under the current constitution, the president is primarily responsible for foreign policy, defense, and national security, while the prime minister oversees domestic policy. After Ben Ali’s removal in January 2011, prime minister Mohamed Ghannouchi invoked Article 56 of the Constitution to assume the role of acting president, a move later declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court, which then appointed Fouad Mebazaa as acting president under Article 57. On 12 December 2011, Moncef Marzouki was elected by the Constituent Assembly as interim president. Presidential elections are held in the last sixty days of the previous term, with candidates required to be Tunisian nationals aged at least 35 and of Muslim faith, who must renounce prior nationality upon election. Voting occurs in two rounds: if no candidate achieves an absolute majority in the first round, a second round is held within two weeks, with the candidate receiving the most votes between the top two advancing. If a candidate dies during the campaign, a new call for candidates is issued within 45 days; this does not apply to candidate withdrawals. The Constitution also prohibits any president from serving more than two full terms, consecutive or non-consecutive, and if a president resigns, the term is considered fully completed.
